questions.stem: For the input “running,” method A mechanically removes the final letters “ing,” producing “runn.” Method B uses the supplied verb part of speech and a lexicon to select the base form “run.” Which classification follows these stated procedures?
assumptions: The algorithms are defined in the stem; no NLTK corpus, library model or original notebook was downloaded or executed.

options.text: Both are stemming, because both outputs are shorter than the input.
A is lemmatization; B is suffix-based stemming.
A is suffix-based stemming; B is lemmatization.
Both are lemmatization, because both remove an inflectional ending.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 45: Week 10 Q1, two illustrative outputs and method explanation
citations.evidenceText: A→runn; B→run; stemming removes endings mechanically and may produce a non-word, while lemmatization produces the meaningful base form.

solution.justification: The procedure, not just whether a word becomes shorter, defines the distinction. “runn” is a supplied illustrative suffix-strip result, not a claim about a named library stemmer.

optionExplanations.o1: Mechanical affix removal is stemming; lexicon/POS-informed base-form selection is lemmatization.
optionExplanations.o2: This reverses the methods’ specified mechanisms.
optionExplanations.o3: Shorter output alone does not distinguish them; B explicitly uses lexical and grammatical information.
optionExplanations.o4: Removing an ending does not establish a valid lexical lemma; A’s rule is explicitly mechanical.

solution.simpleExplanation: The procedure, not just whether a word becomes shorter, defines the distinction. “runn” is a supplied illustrative suffix-strip result, not a claim about a named library stemmer.
misconceptions: This reverses the methods’ specified mechanisms.

questions.stem: In an ASR→LLM→TTS pipeline, the LLM receives only the transcript and TTS receives only the generated reply text. ASR transcribes “turn right” as “turn light.” Which conclusion is warranted even if the later stages faithfully process their own inputs?
assumptions: No original audio or independent confirmation is supplied to the LLM/TTS stages; the question concerns possible propagation, not guaranteed failure on every example.

options.text: A grammatically valid LLM reply establishes that the ASR transcript preserved the intended request.
High-fidelity TTS pronunciation establishes that the original spoken command was transcribed accurately.
A mistaken word can alter the LLM’s interpreted request, and clear synthesized speech may faithfully express the resulting wrong reply.
Separately trained ASR and LLM parameters make this input error irrelevant to the LLM response.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 48: Week 10 Q8, pipeline and right/light transcription example
citations.evidenceText: ASR→LLM→TTS; turn right incorrectly transcribed as turn light.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 49: Week 10 Q8 continuation, cumulative-error explanation
citations.evidenceText: Transcription errors from ASR can cascade into the LLM.

solution.justification: Serial data dependencies allow recognition errors to propagate. Context might help detect an error, but neither fluency nor TTS accuracy guarantees recovery.

optionExplanations.o1: A downstream stage can be accurate relative to a corrupted input while the overall interaction is wrong.
optionExplanations.o2: Grammatical fluency does not certify that the input words match the user’s utterance.
optionExplanations.o3: TTS fidelity evaluates speech rendering of reply text, not correctness of upstream recognition.
optionExplanations.o4: Different parameter sets do not break the data dependency created by passing the transcript onward.

solution.simpleExplanation: Serial data dependencies allow recognition errors to propagate. Context might help detect an error, but neither fluency nor TTS accuracy guarantees recovery.
misconceptions: Grammatical fluency does not certify that the input words match the user’s utterance.

questions.stem: All pretrained CNN backbone parameters are held fixed while only a newly attached classifier’s parameters are optimized on a new task. In the assignment’s terminology, which strategy is this?
assumptions: Classification is based on which parameters are optimized; no claim about batch-normalization buffers or an actual training run is made.

options.text: Partial fine-tuning of the pretrained backbone.
Fixed feature extraction with classifier training.
Full fine-tuning of the pretrained backbone.
Training a newly initialized backbone from scratch.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 49: Week 10 Q9, frozen pretrained CNN and trained classifier
citations.evidenceText: Feature extraction trains only the classifier while retaining the pretrained feature extractor.

solution.justification: A trainable classifier does not imply that the pretrained feature extractor is being fine-tuned.

optionExplanations.o1: The pretrained representation is retained while a new task-specific head learns from it.
optionExplanations.o2: Partial backbone fine-tuning would update at least some pretrained backbone parameters.
optionExplanations.o3: Full fine-tuning would update the backbone broadly rather than keep every backbone parameter fixed.
optionExplanations.o4: The backbone is pretrained and fixed, not newly initialized and optimized.

questions.stem: Two users both say “I finished the assignment,” but their stored histories respectively say “I was struggling” and “I found it easy.” To isolate the effect of retrieved history on a dialogue model’s response, which comparison changes only that factor?
assumptions: Controlled hypothetical evaluation; fix emotion input and deterministic decoding behavior when isolating memory; no live user profiling or model execution.

options.text: Change the current sentence and retrieved history together, while fixing model weights.
Use the same current sentence, model, decoding settings and emotion input; swap only the retrieved history.
Use different random decoding seeds and different histories, while keeping the current sentence fixed.
Use the same current sentence and history, but change the estimated emotion input.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 49: Week 10 Q10, identical new sentence, different prior experiences and memory explanation
citations.evidenceText: UserA struggled; UserB found it easy; identical sentence I finished the assignment. Stored context and estimated emotions are jointly used to plan a response.

solution.justification: The full context can differ despite identical new words. Holding other inputs fixed isolates that difference; it does not establish a person’s true internal emotion.

optionExplanations.o1: Only retrieved history changes, so it is the controlled input difference in this comparison.
optionExplanations.o2: This tests the emotion input rather than the retrieved-history input.
optionExplanations.o3: Changing two semantic inputs prevents isolation of the history effect.
optionExplanations.o4: Changing stochastic decoding as well as history introduces another source of response variation.
